scope_note: Full-source boundary-date probe for four records. Bodies, metadata constraints, excluded layers, footnotes and Airy figure assets were checked; candidate links remain unaccepted and missing antecedents are not reconstructed.

record_reviews.summary: Airy sends a sustained, self-described first sketch based on English plant observations and physical oak-gall models. He moves from alternate distichous 1/2 and 1/3 arrangements through the convergent 2/5, 3/8, 5/13 series, argues that compression and economy of bud space can generate stable orders, then separates longitudinal and lateral contraction to explain spiral versus whorled orders. The final section becomes explicitly speculative, asking whether leaves, ovules, buds, twigs and the whole tree are homologous, while conceding that the wider claim is weak and asking to be judged on leaf order; the postscript offers a demonstration of the models. Five preserved figures were opened: numbered oak-gall packing, simple collateral/alternate forms, and the irregular/alternate/collateral scheme are visible; no prose is inferred from the images beyond this rendering check.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Header reads “From Hubert Airy [before 15] July 1872”; XML sent bounds are 1809-01-01 through 1872-07-14. Footnote dates the letter by Airy’s later reference to receiving Darwin’s letter dated the 15th. This is a broad boundary probe, not a secure 1858–1859 source.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Airy is the author of the surviving 53 body blocks. The salutation is excluded; Darwin pencil annotations and editorial footnotes are separate apparatus, and the figures are Airy’s models/diagrams. No Darwin response is preserved here.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is incoming evidence to Darwin, but no Darwin reply or exact incoming prompt is in this packet; the later Airy correspondence mentioned in the apparatus is not treated as a 1858–1859 answer.

evidence.quote: In laying before you the opinions which I have been led to form concerning the probable origin of the existing orders of Leaf-arrangement
In short, the only stable orders which will arise by compression of the system shown in Fig. 1. are those defined by the convergent series
Have we, in these facts, a hint that the original form of vegetable life was nothing more than a leaf

issues: Five preserved figure assets were visually inspected; they show Airy’s numbered packing/model diagrams and labelled phyllotaxy arrangements.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s two-block copy is a procedural forwarding note. He says that, if George Airy considers it right to communicate Hubert’s paper, Darwin will do so and hopes it will be printed; the closing is only “Signed Ch Darwin”. It contains no account of phyllotaxy itself and no answer to a scientific question.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Header reads “To Hubert Airy [before 21 January 1873]”; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 through 1873-01-20. The copy description and supplied before-date are metadata constraints, outside the nominal period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored copy; the excluded salutation and “Copy” label are apparatus, not body evidence. “Sir Geo Airy” is a named third party, while the paper belongs to Hubert Airy.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No incoming prompt is preserved in this record. The note records a planned Royal Society communication, so it cannot establish that the paper was printed, received, or read by Darwin in the period.

evidence.quote: If Sir Geo Airy thinks it was right to communicate your paper I shall be happy to do so, & I sincerely hope it may be printed.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Bowman to read a slip copied from Donders, asks for analogous clinical cases, and reasons about tears, orbicular spasm, sudden inflammation, yawning, and violent scratching/tickling. The postscript makes the observational request concrete but acknowledges that Darwin does not know whether scratching produces tears and would need a sympathetic medical intermediary. The Donders text is an enclosed reported/translated source, not Bowman’s voice and not a new Bowman letter.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Header reads “To William Bowman [before 26] January [1871]”; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 through 1871-01-25. The footnote establishes the date relationally to a Bowman letter of 26 January 1871; the raw lower bound is open metadata, and no receipt date is given.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing, seven retained blocks. Donders is quoted through Darwin’s enclosure; Bowman is the addressee. The excluded salutation is not body prose.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The letter initiates questions and points to a copied Donders report. It is not itself a response, and the later Bowman record 5338 is explicitly dated by a different Darwin enquiry of 25 January 1872; the one-year date difference and missing enquiry prevent a direct pairing.

evidence.quote: Will you kindly read over the enclosed slip, copied from a long & very valuable letter received some time ago from Donders.
the secretion of tears stands in some very close relation with the spasmodic action of the orbicular muscles
Whether tears are at same time secreted I know not.

record_reviews.summary: Bowman answers a missing Darwin enquiry in a long clinical discussion. He uses dust, corneal ulcer and photophobia, accommodation strain from small print, and distinctions among conjunctiva/cornea, ciliary apparatus, retina, choroid and sclerotica to explain when lacrimation accompanies irritation or inflammation and when it does not. He closes by offering to observe whatever Darwin specifies, while identifying himself as practitioner and anatomist/physiologist and affirming development. The many lacunae are preserved within otherwise surviving paragraphs; the missing Darwin question is not reconstructed.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Header reads “From William Bowman [before 25 January 1872]”; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 through 1872-01-24. Footnote dates it from Darwin’s letter of enquiry of 25 January 1872, which has not been found. No receipt or reading date for Darwin is demonstrated.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Bowman-authored incoming, ten retained blocks, with bracketed editorial restorations/lacunae in the transcription. Bowman’s practitioner/anatomist voice is distinct; the final development remark is his own, not Darwin’s. Darwin annotations and editorial notes do not supply the missing prompt.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: A substantive answer exists but its antecedent is missing. The contents overlap the general tear/eye subject of 7452, yet 7452 asks about Donders, orbicular spasm and tickling in January 1871, whereas Bowman’s apparatus identifies a separate 25 January 1872 enquiry; topic overlap alone is insufficient for a link.

evidence.quote: If a particle of dust irritates the front of the eye, the eye waters
the same inflammation may be attended at one time with much watering, at another time with none at all
if you will let me know what you want me to try to observe I will gladly be a student to help you in my little field.

unlocated_references.description: Bowman’s footnote identifies Darwin’s 25 January 1872 enquiry, but that incoming/outgoing prompt is not preserved in this packet or reconstructed from 7452.
Airy’s apparatus refers to a severely damaged 7 June 1872 letter and a later Airy letter; neither is used as a paired prompt here.

issues: All four records carry open lower XML bounds from 1809 and are period_selection_eligible=false; their supplied dates are 1871–1873 boundary probes, not 1858–1859 eligibility.
5338 and 7452 share eye/tear subject matter but have distinct apparatus dates and distinct missing enquiries; no relationship is proposed.
